title: "QMSR, ISO 13485, and the Vendor"

## Three threads on the same desk

VAL-1203 keeps generating paperwork. This week it's the vendor's formal release package for
Release B: release notes, a revision history, hardware and peripheral specifications, and a list
the vendor calls "unresolved anomalies" — known defects in the current build, each with a short
note on what it does and how bad it is. One entry on that list describes a label-reprint edge
case: if a unit's quarantine status changes in the same second a label reprint is requested at a
satellite site, the reprint can occasionally carry the prior status text for a few seconds before
refreshing. Low frequency, the vendor says, and already scheduled for a future patch. Lakeshore
uses label reprints at Brookfield and Fairview routinely. Nobody on the validation team has
mentioned this entry since it arrived. It's sitting in a folder.

A second thread is older, and nobody's resolved it either. The in-house LIS-to-BECS (laboratory
information system to Blood Establishment Computer Software) translation script — Lakeshore IT's
own Category 5 component, carried in this course since module 1 — reformats result messages
before BECS ever sees them. It isn't sold. Nobody outside Lakeshore has ever looked at a line of
it. Your systems administrator asked, half-joking, in a planning meeting: "If we're writing code
that feeds BECS, are we basically building a medical device at this point?" Nobody answered him.

Then, in the same meeting, your CIO (chief information officer) says something with total
confidence: "Since February 2026, Lakeshore has to comply with the QMSR (Quality Management
System Regulation) and ISO 13485, same as any other device-adjacent company. We should budget
for it next cycle." Heads nod. You don't nod. You've learned, across three modules now, to check
a confident regulatory claim before it becomes a line item.

All three threads point at the same question this module exists to answer: which quality rules
actually bind BECS's manufacturer, which bind Lakeshore, and what do you do with a vendor's
quality-system paperwork once it lands on your desk — read it, file it, or act on it?

## Why this distinction exists, and the ITSM bridge

The failure this module heads off isn't dramatic. It's a vendor's anomaly list arriving, looking
official, and going straight into a folder nobody reopens before sign-off — while a risk
assessment and test plan get written as if the list never existed. The anomaly is real,
documented, even annotated with a safety/effectiveness judgment. And it never touches the one
place it could do some good: VAL-1203's own risk assessment and test design.

You already run the fix for this failure mode under a different name. **ITIL's known error
database (KEDB)** is exactly this idea: a team's own running record of known, not-yet-fixed
defects, each with its workaround and assessed impact, kept so the next person troubleshooting a
symptom doesn't rediscover it from scratch. The vendor's **unresolved-anomalies list** is the same
instrument, built for the same reason, by a different team: a record of what's broken in the build
you're about to install, what it affects, and how bad it is. **Release notes versus revision
history** is the same pairing again — a log of what changed and when, read by whoever has to
reason about what might break next.

Here's where the regulated world asks more of you than an ordinary vendor relationship does. In
routine IT operations, a vendor's KEDB is a courtesy — useful, sometimes incomplete, never
something you'd build your own change plan around without double-checking it yourself. For BECS,
it's different for a specific reason: the vendor's own quality system, the one that produced that
anomaly list, is itself federally regulated. That doesn't make the list more trustworthy on
faith. It makes it a legitimate validation **input** Lakeshore is entitled to ask for and use —
while Lakeshore's own validation obligation, and Lakeshore's own determination of whether the
system is fit to run, stays exactly where it's always been: with Lakeshore.

## The rule in plain English

**First: the QMSR is Part 820, amended — not a new, separate rule.** "QMSR" stands for Quality
Management System Regulation, and it is the current name of 21 CFR Part 820, the device-quality
regulation this curriculum has pointed to since module 3 without quoting its substance. FDA
finalized a rule retitling and restructuring Part 820 — "Medical Devices; Quality System
Regulation Amendments," published February 2, 2024, effective February 2, 2026 — and that
effective date has now arrived in this course's own calendar. Part 820's section header, in the
current text, literally reads "QUALITY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM REGULATION." There is no separate QMSR
statute sitting next to Part 820. It's the same regulation, under its current name.

**Second: Part 820 incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference, rather than restating its content.**
ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 13485 is an international standard for
medical-device quality management systems. FDA doesn't copy ISO 13485's text into the CFR
(Code of Federal Regulations); it names the standard and makes compliance with it the top-line
requirement. That's why this course has described ISO 13485 all along as "named, not quoted" —
it's copyrighted, and the CFR itself only references it by clause number and title, never
reproduces what a clause says.

**Third: 820.10(a)'s top-line requirement is to document a quality management system that
complies with ISO 13485.** Everything else in 820.10 is detail hung off that one sentence,
including a class-specific requirement that matters directly here: manufacturers of Class II
devices — and BECS is Class II, established back in module 3 — must comply with ISO 13485's
Design and Development clause and its subclauses. BECS's manufacturer doesn't get to treat design
controls as optional.

**Fourth: 820.3 defines "manufacturer" and "finished device" in terms of what something does, not
who sells it or what it's called.** A manufacturer is defined by activity — designing,
manufacturing, fabricating, assembling, processing a finished device — not by having a storefront
or a sales contract. And a "finished device" explicitly includes "any device **or accessory to
any device**" that's suitable for use, whether or not it's packaged or labeled. That "accessory"
language is the same word 864.9165(a) used in module 3 to describe a "BECS accessory" — something
that augments BECS's performance or expands what it's cleared to do. Keep that word in mind; it's
the hinge the in-house-script question turns on, below.

**Fifth, and the central legal fact of this whole course: 820.1(a)(3) excludes blood and blood
component manufacturers from Part 820 entirely.** Lakeshore, as a manufacturer of blood and blood
components for transfusion, isn't a "manufacturer" Part 820/QMSR reaches at all — it answers
instead to Subchapter F, the blood-specific regulations this course has cited from the start
(Part 606, and Part 211 as it supplements, per module 1's 210.2(a)). Part 820, including the QMSR
and the ISO 13485 it incorporates, binds **BECS's manufacturer** — the vendor, as the entity that
designs and builds the device. It was never going to bind Lakeshore, no matter what the calendar
says.

**Sixth: those same definitions make the in-house-script question genuinely hard, not easy.** Your
sysadmin's half-joking question — "if we're writing code that feeds BECS, are we basically
building a medical device?" — deserves a straight answer, and the straight answer is that this
course doesn't have one, and neither does anyone without more to go on than what's locally
verified. 820.3's "finished device" reaches "any device or accessory to any device." 864.9165(a)
— quoted in full back in module 3 — defines a "BECS accessory" as a device intended for use with
BECS "to augment the performance of the BECS or to expand or modify its indications for use."
Does reformatting LIS result messages into BECS's expected input format "augment the performance
of BECS," the way the accessory language means it? Or is it simply plumbing between two other
systems, never touching BECS's own indications for use? Arguments exist on both sides, and none
resolve cleanly from text this course has verified. The script isn't sold, which cuts against a
classic "manufacturer" picture built around commerce — but 820.3's definition is built on
activity, not a sale, so "nobody's paying for it" isn't a clean exit either. It isn't BECS's own
code, and the vendor had no hand in it — but an "accessory" under 864.9165(a) is explicitly a
*separate* device from BECS itself, so being separate doesn't settle the question in Lakeshore's
favor on its own terms. Whether this script crosses the line FDA means by "accessory" is a
judgment call resting on facts and interpretation this course has no verified source to make for
you — which is exactly why it's routed, not resolved, below.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 820.1(a)(3) | "Eight-twenty point one, paragraph a, subparagraph three" | Excludes manufacturers of blood and blood components from Part 820/QMSR; they answer to Subchapter F instead. | Refutes the CIO's claim directly. Lakeshore is excluded by name. |
| 21 CFR 820.7(b) | "Eight-twenty point seven, paragraph b" | Incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference into Part 820, approved for §§ 820.1, 820.3, 820.10, 820.35, and 820.45. | The mechanism by which an international standard becomes binding on a device manufacturer without the CFR restating its text. |
| 21 CFR 820.3 | "Eight-twenty point three" | Defines "manufacturer" by activity, and "finished device" to include accessories. | The definitions the in-house-script question has to be tested against — unresolved here, routed below. |
| 21 CFR 820.10(a) | "Eight-twenty point ten, paragraph a" | Top-line requirement: document a QMS complying with ISO 13485. | What Release B's manufacturer has to have, full stop, as a Class II device maker. |
| 21 CFR 820.10(c) | "Eight-twenty point ten, paragraph c" | Class II and III manufacturers must comply with ISO 13485's Design and Development clause and subclauses. | BECS is Class II (module 3). This binds the vendor's design process for Release B. |
| 21 CFR 820.10(b)(3)/(4) | "Eight-twenty point ten, paragraph b, subparagraphs three and four" | Complaints meeting reporting criteria go to FDA under Part 803; advisory notices follow Part 806. | Named here because the section itself is saved; Parts 803/806's own text is out of scope for this lesson. |
| 21 CFR 864.9165(b)(1)-(5) | "Eight sixty-four point ninety-one sixty-five, paragraph b, subparagraphs one through five" | The five special controls for BECS as a Class II device: software specs, V&V testing, labeling (including the anomaly list and revision history), the traceability matrix, performance testing. | The vendor deliverables sitting in VAL-1203's folder right now — the anomaly list and traceability matrix by name. |

## The actual text

Start with the fact that settles the CIO's claim, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/820.1.md`:

> (3) Blood and blood components. The provisions of this part do not apply to manufacturers of
> blood and blood components used for transfusion or for further manufacturing. Such manufacturers
> are subject to subchapter F of this chapter.

Lakeshore manufactures blood and blood components. This paragraph names that activity by name and
excludes it. Not "exempt under certain conditions." Excluded, full stop, from this part.

The incorporation mechanism, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/820.7.md`:

> (b) ISO 13485:2016(E) ("ISO 13485"), Medical devices—Quality management systems—Requirements for
> regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016; IBR approved for §§ 820.1, 820.3, 820.10,
> 820.35, and 820.45.

IBR means "incorporated by reference" — a standard FDA has adopted into the regulation's text
without reprinting it. That's why ISO 13485 appears throughout 820's sections as clause numbers
and titles, never as quoted content.

The top-line requirement, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/820.10.md`:

> (a) Document. Document a quality management system that complies with the applicable
> requirements of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) and other applicable
> requirements of this part; and

The class-specific design requirement, same section:

> (c) Design and development. Manufacturers of class II, class III, and those class I devices
> listed in paragraph (c)(1) of this section and table 1 to paragraph (c)(2) of this section must
> comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its Subclauses in ISO
> 13485.

BECS is Class II. This paragraph reaches Release B's manufacturer directly, by classification,
with no ambiguity.

Named here because the section itself is a saved source, even though Parts 803 and 806 aren't
(go no further than this text says):

> (3) For Clause 8.2.3 in ISO 13485, Reporting to regulatory authorities, the manufacturer must
> notify FDA of complaints that meet the reporting criteria of part 803 of this chapter.
>
> (4) For Clauses 7.2.3, 8.2.3, and 8.3.3, advisory notices shall be handled in accordance with the
> requirements of part 806 of this chapter.

The definitions the in-house-script question will turn on, quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/820.3.md`:

> Manufacturer means any person who designs, manufactures, fabricates, assembles, or processes a
> finished device. Manufacturer includes, but is not limited to, those who perform the functions
> of contract sterilization, installation, relabeling, remanufacturing, repacking, or
> specification development, and initial distributors of foreign entities performing these
> functions.

> Finished device means any device or accessory to any device that is suitable for use or capable
> of functioning, whether or not it is packaged, labeled, or sterilized.

And the five special controls binding Release B's manufacturer as a Class II device, quoted
verbatim and in full from `sources/cfr/864.9165.md` — module 3 quoted only the classification
line; this is the text that follows it:

> (1) Software performance and functional requirements including detailed design specifications
> (e.g., algorithms or control characteristics, alarms, device limitations, and safety
> requirements).
>
> (2) Verification and validation testing and hazard analysis must be performed.
>
> (3) Labeling must include:
>
> (i) Software limitations;
>
> (ii) Unresolved anomalies, annotated with an explanation of the impact on safety or
> effectiveness;
>
> (iii) Revision history; and
>
> (iv) Hardware and peripheral specifications.
>
> (4) Traceability matrix must be performed.
>
> (5) Performance testing to ensure the safety and effectiveness of the system must be performed,
> including when adding new functional requirements (e.g., electrical safety, electromagnetic
> compatibility, or wireless coexistence).

Read (3)(ii) and (4) against the folder on your desk. The anomaly list and its explanation of
safety/effectiveness impact is a *regulatory requirement on the vendor's labeling* — not a courtesy
document. So is the traceability matrix the vendor ships with its own V&V evidence. These are
**vendor deliverables**: things Release B's manufacturer is required to produce, as part of its
own, separately regulated quality system. FDA's BECS guidance has told you since module 1 that
you're "ultimately responsible" for your own validation. These deliverables don't change that.
They give that validation better raw material to work with.

That's where GAMP 5's (the ISPE's industry-practice framework this course has used since module 1)
own emphasis matters, paraphrased only: the current edition leans on leveraging supplier
documentation as a normal, expected part of a well-run validation — not a shortcut around doing
your own, but a recognition that a vendor's own tested output is a real input your risk
assessment and test plan should actually use. The label-reprint anomaly sitting in a folder,
unread, is the opposite of that practice. Fed into VAL-1203's risk assessment, it's a specific,
named failure mode Lakeshore now knows to test for at the exact boundary condition the vendor
described — precisely the Coverage question module 2 taught you to ask of any high-risk function.

Now the "software as a medical device" framing, and where it comes from. FDA's own term for
software that itself meets the device definition is **"device software functions"** — quoted
directly from `sources/fda-guidance/csa-production-qms-software-2026-excerpt.md`:

> This guidance does not provide recommendations for the design and development verification or
> validation requirements for device software functions, which are software functions that meet
> the definition of a device under section 201(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
> (FD&C Act).

BECS is a device software function. **SaMD** (Software as a Medical Device) is the international
umbrella term for this same idea, coined by **IMDRF** (International Medical Device Regulators
Forum) — name it as the field's shorthand and nothing more. No IMDRF definition is quoted or
asserted here; none has been verified against a saved source, so none is claimed.

The sentence above comes from a guidance worth naming precisely, because it's easy to misapply:
**Computer Software Assurance for Production and Quality Management System Software** (the CSA
guidance, CDRH/CBER, final, issue date 02/03/2026). Its own scope excludes device software
functions by name — it's written for software a device *manufacturer* uses in its own production
and quality-management systems, not for the device software itself. It also discusses ISO 13485's
Subclauses 4.1.6, 7.5.6, and 7.6 — named here only as bare numbers appearing inside FDA's own
guidance text, not described further; ISO 13485's actual content stays off-limits. A separate,
older guidance, *General Principles of Software Validation* (2002, CDRH/CBER), is the one FDA's
own BECS guidance points a device manufacturer to for validating its *own* device software — named
here only, already sourced in earlier modules.

One AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) mention, paraphrase only, no
standard number: this whole terrain — what you can reasonably expect from a supplier, and how that
relationship gets managed — sits under **QSE 4, Suppliers and Customers**, in AABB's Quality
System Essentials framework.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor reading VAL-1203's file wouldn't ask whether Lakeshore holds
an ISO 13485 certificate — it's the wrong question. They'd ask three things instead.

**Evidence the vendor's anomaly list and traceability matrix were actually used, not just filed.**
A dated note in the risk assessment referencing the specific anomaly, a test case added to address
the boundary condition it describes, or a documented decision that the risk is acceptable as-is —
any of these shows the deliverable did its job. A folder with an unopened PDF in it doesn't.

**A written record of the in-house-script question, routed somewhere real.** Not a hallway
conversation, not a line in a meeting's minutes that nobody followed up on. A document: here's the
question, here's who it went to, here's what regulatory affairs said or when they're expected to
say it.

**Nobody in the file asserting that Lakeshore itself is QMSR-bound.** If VAL-1203's background
section ever picked up a sentence like the CIO's — "Lakeshore complies with the QMSR" — that's a
mischaracterization of Lakeshore's own regulatory status, in a document meant to survive an
inspector's cold read.

A bad answer to "what did you do with the vendor's anomaly list" sounds like "we have it on file."
A good answer points to the specific line in the risk assessment it fed.

## Common traps

**"Since the QMSR took effect, Lakeshore has to comply with it and ISO 13485, like any other
device-adjacent company."** This is the CIO's exact claim, and 820.1(a)(3) answers it directly:
Lakeshore manufactures blood and blood components, and the provision excludes exactly that
activity from Part 820, in favor of Subchapter F. "Device-adjacent" isn't a status Part 820
recognizes. You either manufacture a finished device (or an accessory to one) or you don't, and
blood manufacturers are named out by paragraph, not left to argue the point.

**"The vendor's special-control deliverables are the vendor's business, not ours to read
closely."** Also wrong, in the other direction. 864.9165(b)(3)(ii) and (b)(4) exist because FDA
requires them of the manufacturer — but nothing stops Lakeshore from using them, and FDA's own
"ultimately responsible" framing (named in module 3) means Lakeshore's validation is stronger, not
weaker, for actually reading them. Treating a vendor deliverable as none of Lakeshore's concern
wastes a regulatory requirement someone else already paid to satisfy.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask the vendor for its unresolved-anomalies list, revision history, and traceability matrix as
  a matter of course on every upgrade — not just because they might hand them over, but because
  864.9165(b) requires the vendor to produce them.** Then prove you read them: a dated line in the
  risk assessment, not a filed PDF.
- **When an anomaly touches a function Lakeshore actually uses, treat it as a named test case, not
  background noise.** The label-reprint entry belongs in VAL-1203's test plan at the exact boundary
  condition the vendor described — that's Coverage, from module 2, applied to a vendor's own
  documented failure mode instead of one Lakeshore discovered independently.
- **Correct a "we're QMSR-bound now" claim the moment you hear it, with the citation in hand.**
  820.1(a)(3) is a short paragraph. Keep it ready — this is exactly the kind of confident,
  plausible-sounding claim that gets into a budget line or a validation plan's background section
  before anyone checks it.
- **Never let a vendor's own compliance with Part 820/ISO 13485 substitute for Lakeshore's
  validation.** The same shared-responsibility logic module 3 applied to 510(k) clearance applies
  here, one layer up: a compliant vendor quality system is real, and it's an input. It was never a
  stand-in for VAL-1203's own evidence.
- **If anyone — IT, a consultant, even you — raises whether an in-house-built component makes
  Lakeshore a "manufacturer," write the question down precisely and send it to regulatory
  affairs, rather than guessing.** Name what the script does, what data it touches, that it's
  built and maintained entirely in-house, and the exact regulatory language in tension (820.3's
  "manufacturer" and "finished device," 864.9165(a)'s "BECS accessory"). That's not the Director's
  call to make, or the Quality Validation Lead's either, however confident either of you might
  feel after this module — it's a question a regulatory affairs professional is positioned to
  research properly, potentially with FDA itself, and it's better asked precisely in writing now
  than guessed at by whoever's in the room when it comes up.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your CIO says, "Since February 2026, Lakeshore has to comply with the QMSR and ISO 13485, same as any other device-adjacent company." Accurate?

No. 21 CFR 820.1(a)(3) is explicit: "The provisions of this part do not apply to manufacturers of
blood and blood components used for transfusion or for further manufacturing. Such manufacturers
are subject to subchapter F of this chapter." Lakeshore manufactures blood and blood components,
so it's named out of Part 820/QMSR entirely, not left in some in-between "device-adjacent"
category. Lakeshore answers to blood CGMP (21 CFR Part 606, with Part 211 as it supplements, per
module 1) and FDA's BECS user-facility guidance instead. The QMSR and ISO 13485 bind BECS's
*manufacturer* — the vendor — not Lakeshore.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Does Lakeshore become a "manufacturer" under 820.3 by building and maintaining the LIS-to-BECS translation script in-house?

This course can't answer that, and says so honestly. 820.3 defines "finished device" to include
"any device or accessory to any device," and 864.9165(a) defines a "BECS accessory" as something
that augments BECS's performance or expands its indications for use. Whether a script that
reformats data flowing into BECS — not sold, not BECS's own code, built entirely in-house — meets
that definition is a real interpretive question, and nothing in this curriculum's verified sources
settles it either way. The correct move is to write the question down precisely (what the script
does, what it touches, the exact regulatory language in tension) and route it to Lakeshore's
regulatory affairs function. Not something the Director or the Validation Lead should guess at.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: The vendor's unresolved-anomalies list has one entry touching a function Lakeshore actually uses. What should happen to it?

It should feed VAL-1203's risk assessment and test plan directly — not sit in a folder as proof the
vendor disclosed something. 864.9165(b)(3)(ii) requires the vendor to label unresolved anomalies
"annotated with an explanation of the impact on safety or effectiveness," which means the vendor
has already done real analysis on this defect. Module 2's Coverage question (does every requirement
touching a critical function trace to a real test?) applies here with a vendor-supplied failure
mode instead of one Lakeshore found on its own: the anomaly's exact boundary condition belongs in
the test plan as a named case. Using it this way is industry practice (GAMP 5's own emphasis on
leveraging supplier documentation), not a regulatory mandate on Lakeshore — but ignoring a
documented, vendor-identified failure mode that touches your own operations is the kind of gap an
inspector finds fast.
:::

## Where this goes next

You now know exactly where the line sits: Part 820/QMSR and ISO 13485 bind Release B's
manufacturer, 820.1(a)(3) keeps Lakeshore out of that part entirely, and the vendor's special-
control deliverables are real validation inputs, never substitutes. What you haven't pinned down
yet is what Part 11 (electronic records and signatures) actually requires *your* validation to
prove the system enforces, and whether a vendor-supported, remotely-accessed BECS still counts as
a "closed system" under FDA's rules. That's `part-11-for-validated-systems`, next.
